story_pergunta: At your company, who approves the extensions your devs install?

slides.eyebrow: AI ON THE RISE · AGENT SUPPLY CHAIN
slides.headline: Your coding agent is only as safe as its extensions
slides.sub: A backdoored Claude Code extension hit the Cursor Marketplace.

slides.headline: A tampered Claude Code extension shipped with an SSH backdoor
slides.body: Phorion detected a backdoor in the Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace. Cursor removed versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313. The payload runs as soon as the file loads, with no user interaction needed.

slides.label: developer systems impacted, according to Cursor
slides.sub: Figure as reported by DoublePulsar, citing Cursor.

slides.headline: What I see in companies adopting coding agents
items: Extensions install and auto-update, and nobody owns the approved list
Agents and IDEs run with the full access of the developer's machine
Nothing sits between a new tool and production code or credentials

slides.headline: How the AskMoses.AI development team works with agents
items: Every dev works with Claude Code on the project
Another Claude reviews the pull request before it moves on
The human decides on business grounds, not technical ones
Deploys on Vercel with 1-click rollback and daily backups

slides.headline: Launching is not the same as being used.
slides.body: This also applies to safety. An allowlist, least-privilege access and a review gate only matter if they are enforced every day. A policy nobody follows is not a control. Measure what your agents can reach, instead of assuming.

slides.eyebrow: WANT TO SEE HOW I DID IT?
slides.headline: Comment CLAUDE.
slides.body: I'll send you the step-by-step of this case by DM. I take AI off the drawing board and put it into production, with measured results.

caption:
A backdoored version of the Claude Code extension showed up on the Cursor Marketplace. Phorion detected it. The payload tries to plant an SSH key, open a reverse tunnel and persist across reboots. Cursor removed versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 and, per DoublePulsar, put the number of impacted developer systems at around 5,000.

What strikes me is not the malware itself. It is where it got in. Extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user, so a compromised one reaches local files, source code and developer tooling.

In practice, what I see in companies is simple. Nobody owns the list of approved extensions. Agents run with broad access. And nothing sits between a new tool and production.

On the AskMoses.AI development team, every dev works with Claude Code, another Claude reviews the pull request, and the human decides on business grounds. Deploys go through Vercel with 1-click rollback and daily backups.

If you ship with agents, you need an allowlist, least-privilege access and a review gate before anything touches production.

Comment CLAUDE and I'll DM you how I did it.

Sources: phorion.io, doublepulsar.com
